details:
**Wu wei**
The central Daoist ideal of "effortless action," "non-action," or "action through inaction": acting in harmony with the natural flow of the Dao instead of forcing outcomes. Chapter 37 of the Daodejing says the Dao "does nothing, yet nothing is left undone," and the economist François Quesnay is said to have rendered the idea as "laissez-faire."

**Zhuangzi's butterfly dream**
The most famous passage of the Zhuangzi, a foundational Daoist text named after its 4th-century BCE author. Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, then wakes and cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming that it is a man.

**Laozi**
The legendary founder of Daoism, whose name means "Old Master." Tradition says he was an archivist at the Zhou royal court who grew tired of society and left China riding a water buffalo (ox), writing down the Daodejing at the request of a border guard before he disappeared.

**Daodejing (Tao Te Ching)**
The central Daoist text, attributed to Laozi and usually translated as "The Book of the Way and Its Virtue." Its 81 short chapters begin "The Dao that can be told is not the eternal Dao; the name that can be named is not the eternal name," and it praises the "mysterious female," the gate from which Heaven and Earth emerge. The saying "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step" also comes from it.

**Yin and yang**
The two complementary opposing forces, such as dark and light or feminine and masculine, whose interplay makes up the universe. They are shown in the taijitu (the yin-yang symbol), which is sometimes surrounded by the eight trigrams of the I Ching ("Book of Changes"), a divination classic that Daoism draws on.

**Three Treasures**
The three virtues of compassion, moderation (frugality), and humility, laid out in chapter 67 of the Daodejing. In internal alchemy, the term also refers to jing (essence), qi (vital energy), and shen (spirit).

**The Vinegar Tasters**
A traditional allegorical painting in which Confucius, the Buddha, and Laozi taste vinegar. Confucius looks sour and the Buddha bitter, while Laozi smiles, showing Daoism's positive acceptance of life as it is.

**Pu (the uncarved block) and ziran**
Pu, the uncarved block of wood, is a Daoist symbol of simplicity and of human nature before society shapes it. It is connected to ziran, "naturalness" or "self-so," the spontaneous way things happen by themselves.

**Other Zhuangzi stories**
The Zhuangzi includes a debate with the logician Huizi about whether one can know the happiness of fish, and Zhuangzi drumming on a tub and singing after his wife's death because death is like the changing of the seasons. It also tells of Cook Ding, whose butchering is so skillful that his knife stays sharp for nineteen years, and of Hundun (Chaos), who dies when two emperors drill the seven openings of the human face into him.

**Jade Emperor**
The supreme ruler of Heaven in popular Daoism, who presides over a celestial bureaucracy. Legend says he chose the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac through a race.

**Three Pure Ones**
The highest deities of religious Daoism, usually shown as elderly men: the Jade Pure One, the Supreme Pure One, and the Grand Pure One (a deified Laozi). One is said to have divided time into epochs, and they are often depicted holding objects such as a fan or a fly whisk.

**Celestial Masters and the Five Pecks of Rice**
The Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organized Daoist religious movement, was founded in the 2nd century CE by Zhang Daoling and was called the Five Pecks of Rice (Wudoumi) movement after its membership dues. Its descendant, Zhengyi Daoism, is one of the two main modern schools; the other is the monastic Quanzhen school, centered at the White Cloud Abbey in Beijing, whose master Qiu Chuji met Genghis Khan.

**Hell Bank Notes and joss paper**
Paper offerings, often printed with the image of the Jade Emperor, that are burned so that they reach ancestors and spirits in the afterlife. They are a modern form of sacrifice in Chinese religion.

**Eight Immortals**
A group of legendary Daoist figures who achieved immortality, often shown together in Chinese art. They include He Xiangu, the only woman among them, who is said to have become immortal by eating powdered mica.

**Pangu**
The giant of Chinese creation myth who hatched from a cosmic egg and separated Heaven and Earth, pushing them apart for 18,000 years. When he died, his body became the features of the world.
